$comment: Module registry for bootstrap.ps1. Pure data - a future POSIX runner reads the same file. Link targets are keyed by platform; a link with no entry for the current platform is skipped.

modules.$comment: Not enabled by default - installing software is a heavier action than dropping a symlink, so it is always an explicit opt-in. Find a package id with `winget search <name>` and use the exact Id column value.

git itself. Circular on a machine that already cloned this repo, but the entry earns its place the moment someone sets one up from a zip or a different clone method
requires.$comment: Upgrading this one is awkward and the failure is opaque. It installs machine-wide, so -Upgrade without elevation gets [ADMIN]. Elevate and it can still fail with a bare 'Installer failed with exit code: 1': the Inno Setup installer refuses while any Git for Windows binary is running, and silent mode takes the suppressed prompt's default, which is Cancel. Claude Code's Bash tool is Git Bash, so a session open in this repo is itself the blocker. Upgrade Git from a shell that is not Git Bash with no Claude Code running, or pass --custom "/CLOSEAPPLICATIONS /RESTARTAPPLICATIONS" and accept that it terminates those shells. The real reason is never on winget's stdout - it is in the installer log winget names on the failing line.

requires.reason: gh - PRs and issues from the terminal
pairs with the nvim config already tracked in this repo, which the nvim module will link once its direction is de-tangled
PowerShell 7. The powershell module links profile.ps1 into PS7's directory once pwsh exists
requires.$comment: Do NOT expect Windows Terminal to add the profile for you, and do not restore that claim: it held while this package was an MSI, but winget's Microsoft.PowerShell manifest switched from the MSI to an msixbundle during 7.5.x (7.5.0 is still wix, 7.5.10 and later are msix), and for the msix the PowershellCore generator produces nothing. Upstream is PowerShell/PowerShell#27064, open, reported as a regression from 7.6.0; microsoft/terminal#2982 and #18618 are the older MSIX-detection reports. So windows-terminal/settings.json carries a static PowerShell profile of its own - see that module's comment for why its commandline is spelled out in full. Consequence of the msix: there is no C:\Program Files\PowerShell\7 on any machine set up after the switch, pwsh lives under C:\Program Files\WindowsApps (ACL locked and version stamped, so never reference it directly) and is reachable only through the app execution alias in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WindowsApps. Passing --installer-type msi does not help; winget answers 'No applicable installer found'. The MSI is still published on PowerShell's GitHub releases if a machine ever genuinely needs a machine-wide install, but nothing here requires elevation as it stands, which is the one thing the msix does better.

modules.$comment: Targets are computed, never hardcoded. Documents on this machine is both redirected to OneDrive and localised - the real path is OneDrive\Documenten - so %USERPROFILE%\Documents would be wrong here and wrong in a different way on another machine. {documents} resolves it correctly under redirection, localisation and neither. The two directory names beneath it are fixed: WindowsPowerShell for 5.1, PowerShell for 7. Do not reach for $PROFILE to derive these - it resolves against whichever host runs the bootstrap, so running it from pwsh would aim both links at the PS7 path and leave Windows PowerShell unlinked. profile.ps1 is the AllHosts profile, so it also loads in the VS Code terminal and the ISE, and one file serves both shells. Machine-local additions go in Microsoft.PowerShell_profile.ps1 beside it, which stays unversioned.

links.$comment: PowerShell 7 reads {documents}\PowerShell, a sibling of Windows PowerShell's directory, and one file serves both. Gated on pwsh rather than on the directory existing: PS7 creates no profile directory until something writes one, so a directory test would answer no on a machine that does have PS7.

modules.todo: Wire up .vimrc, .ideavimrc, .vsvimrc. Supersedes install-vim-windows.cmd, which uses a bare mklink /H with no conflict checking. Note .vimrc currently has no link on this machine.

BLOCKED on de-tangling the link direction first. On the machine where it was set up, the repo's `nvim` entry is itself a symlink pointing OUT to %LOCALAPPDATA%
vim - the opposite direction from every other entry. Git followed it when adding, so 17 real files are tracked at mode 100644 and a fresh clone does get the actual config; content is not at risk. The gap is that a fresh clone leaves nvim/ as an ordinary directory nobody reads, because nothing links %LOCALAPPDATA%
vim to it. Wiring the obvious link here would be self-referential on the original machine, where repo/nvim already points at that exact target. Fix by inverting it there - replace the repo symlink with the real directory, then link %LOCALAPPDATA%
vim back to it - after which the same link works everywhere and this module can be populated.

modules.$comment: The background image is referenced as the relative path assets/terminal_bg.png. Windows Terminal 1.24+ resolves backgroundImage relative to settings.json, so nothing machine-specific is baked into the shared file and no environment variable is needed. Linking the assets directory in alongside settings.json means it resolves whether WT looks beside the symlink or beside the file the symlink points at. 8wekyb3d8bbwe is Microsoft's publisher hash and is constant for Store apps, so the package path needs no globbing. The same constant hash is why the PowerShell profile can hard-code %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WindowsApps\Microsoft.PowerShell_8wekyb3d8bbwe\pwsh.exe. That spelled-out path is load bearing, do not simplify it back to a bare pwsh.exe: the msix ships pwsh only as a 0-byte app execution alias, and Terminal's resolution of a bare executable name does not follow those, so the tab dies with [error 2147942402 (0x80070002)]. An absolute path to that very same alias launches fine. Measured on 1.24.11911.0: absolute per-package alias works, absolute %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WindowsApps\pwsh.exe works, bare pwsh.exe fails, and cmd.exe resolves the bare name happily because its own search does follow the alias. The per-package directory is preferred over the plain alias because it survives the App execution aliases toggle in Settings and cannot be shadowed by another package publishing pwsh.exe. Relatedly the profile is static, with its own guid and no source field, rather than a dynamic profile keyed to Windows.Terminal.PowershellCore; the generator-backed guid {574e775e-4f2a-5b96-ac1e-a2962a402336} is retained but hidden so a machine whose Terminal does still generate it will not show two entries named PowerShell. Only the stable channel is managed: Preview is installed here too but keeps its own settings, and adopting it would mean overwriting a working config - link it deliberately with -Force if you ever want the two channels shared. On a WT older than 1.24 the relative path will not resolve; the fallback is an absolute-free %WT_SETTINGS_DIR%\assets\terminal_bg.png plus an env entry pointing that variable at {repo}\windows-terminal. IMPORTANT: editing settings.json in this repo does NOT hot-reload a running Windows Terminal. WT watches its LocalState directory, and a write to the symlink's target raises no notification there - measured for symlinks, hardlinks, and even writes made through the link. Run `bootstrap.ps1 -Modules windows-terminal -Reload` after editing to nudge it, or restart WT.

requires.reason: settings.json sets font.face to this; without it Windows Terminal silently falls back and the powerline glyphs in the claude-powerline statusline render as boxes. Vendored rather than fetched because winget has no FiraCode Nerd Font package - only JetBrainsMono - and the font is OFL licensed, so redistributing it here is fine
